{{short description|Invariant cord in one of two intersecting circles based on any point in the other}}
[[File:Satz von der konstanten Sehne2.svg|thumb|upright=1.5|constant chord length: <math>|P_1Q_1|=|P_2Q_2|</math>]]
[[File:Satz von der konstanten Sehne 3d.png|thumb|upright=1.5|constant diameter length: <math>|P_1Q_1|=|P_2Q_2|</math>]]
The '''constant chord theorem''' is a statement in elementary [[geometry]] about a property of certain [[Chord (geometry)|chords]] in two intersecting [[circle]]s.

The circles <math>k_1</math> and <math>k_2</math> intersect in the points <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>. <math>Z_1</math> is an arbitrary point on <math>k_1</math> being different from  <math>P</math> and <math>Q</math>. The lines <math>Z_1P</math> and <math>Z_1Q</math> intersect the circle <math>k_2</math> in <math>P_1</math> and <math>Q_1</math>. The constant chord theorem then states that the length of the chord <math>P_1Q_1</math> in <math>k_2</math> does not depend on the location of <math>Z_1</math> on <math>k_1</math>, in other words the length is constant.

The theorem stays valid when <math>Z_1</math> coincides with <math>P</math> or <math>Q</math>, provided one replaces the then undefined line <math>Z_1P</math> or <math>Z_1Q</math> by the tangent on <math>k_1</math> at <math>Z_1</math>. 

A similar theorem exists in three dimensions for the intersection of two [[sphere]]s. The spheres <math>k_1</math> and <math>k_2</math> intersect in the circle <math>k_s</math>. <math>Z_1</math> is arbitrary point on the surface of the first sphere <math>k_1</math>, that is not on the intersection circle <math>k_s</math>. The extended [[cone]] created by <math>k_s</math> and <math>Z_1</math> intersects the second sphere <math>k_2</math> in a circle. The length of the diameter of this circle is constant, that is it does not depend on the location of <math>Z_1</math> on <math>k_1</math>.

[[Nathan Altshiller Court]] described the constant chord theorem 1925 in the article ''sur deux cercles secants'' for the Belgian math journal [[Mathesis (journal)|Mathesis]]. Eight years later he published  ''On Two Intersecting Spheres'' in the [[American Mathematical Monthly]], which contained the 3-dimensional version. Later it was included in several textbooks, such as [[Ross Honsberger]]'s ''Mathematical Morsels'' and [[Roger B. Nelsen]]'s ''Proof Without Words II'', where it was given as a problem, or the German geometry textbook ''Mit harmonischen Verhältnissen zu Kegelschnitten'' by Halbeisen, [[:de:Norbert_Hungerbühler|Hungerbühler]] and Läuchli, where it was given as a theorem.
